decisions.location: Section 3.1 Background and Motivation, p. 10 (lines 734-743); References, p. 47 (lines 4627-4635)
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind target 0 identify the same tested original study: Porretta, Buchanan, & Järvikivi (2020), 'When processing costs impact predictive processing: The case of foreign-accented speech and accent experience'. The authors explicitly state in the Abstract and Section 3.1 that they carried out a single-change (web-based) replication of Porretta et al. (2020)'s in-person visual world paradigm experiment.

decisions.quote:
We demonstrate our

12

approach by carrying out a single change replication of an in-person eye-tracking study,

13

Porretta et al. (2020).
decisions.reason: The authors collected new web-based eye-tracking data from a fresh sample of 60 Prolific participants (49 analyzed after exclusions) using Porretta et al. (2020)'s recordings and design to re-test Porretta et al. (2020)'s findings. Both shipped and blind codings accurately classify the record as a 'replication'.

decisions.location: Section 5.1 Discussion, p. 40, lines 3838-3858 (and Section 3.1, p. 11, lines 825-847; Section 4.3, p. 38, lines 3761-3769; Section 5.1, p. 41, lines 3914-3916)
decisions.quote:
Our replication results indicate that web-based eye-tracking can capture the same

6

predictive processing as in-person eye-tracking (e.g., Prystauka et al., 2023; Vos et al., 2022).

7

Our main models show that predictive sentence processing is modulated by restrictive and

8

non-restrictive verb type in line with Porretta et al. (2020) and that accented speech impedes

9

predictive processing but does not preclude it. Interestingly, our accent models did not find

10

evidence of accent-experience modulating predictive processing.
decisions.reason: Both shipped row 2337 and blind target 0 coded 'mixed' for the replication of Porretta, Buchanan, & Järvikivi (2020, DOI: 10.3758/s13414-019-01946-7), but under Codebook Step 3 Rules 1 and 2 the outcome is 'successful'. First, for Research Question 1 (the main models testing verb restrictiveness and talker accent on predictive sentence processing), the primary source states both Porretta et al.'s original finding and the corresponding replication result, and explicitly concludes that the replication succeeded across both GLMM and GAMM analyses ('We observed nearly identical time course of predictive processing (Figure 11) in which restricted sentences resulted in earlier looks to the target object than nonrestrictive sentences. Further, this effect is partially reduced in accented speech in a similar manner to Porretta et al. (2020)', Section 4.3, lines 3761-3769; 'Our main models show that predictive sentence processing is modulated by restrictive and non-restrictive verb type in line with Porretta et al. (2020) and that accented speech impedes predictive processing but does not preclude it', Section 5.1, lines 3844-3854). Second, for Research Question 2 (the accent-experience models), the primary source lists Porretta et al.'s second research question ('2) To what extent does accent experience modulate prediction in accented speech?', Section 3.1, lines 834-837) and reports Porretta et al.'s sample mean/SD of Chinese accent exposure (1.78, SD = 0.82, Section 3.2.3, lines 1076-1081), but never states what Porretta et al.'s accent-experience analysis actually found. Under Codebook Step 3 Rule 2a ('Two tests before you code from an implicit comparison, and both must pass: (a) the evidence states what THE ORIGINAL THIS OUTCOME IS ABOUT found. You cannot compare against a finding the evidence never states, however positive this paper's own results sound'), a research question is not an original finding, so the accent-experience null cannot establish a failed comparison against Porretta et al. (2020). Moreover, the authors themselves explicitly restrict direct replication comparison to RQ1 in Section 3.1 ('A direct comparison can be made between our study and Porretta et al. (2020) for research question one... For research question two, our interpretation will be limited given our random sample of Prolific participants (i.e., we are not controlling experience with Chinese-accented English)', lines 839-847) and explicitly declare their accent models uninformative/inconclusive due to lower sample exposure, insufficient statistical power (49 analyzed vs. ~90 needed), and slider measurement error in Section 5.1 ('Our results are, therefore, inconclusive with respect to the accent models', p. 41, lines 3914-3916). Because the sole established comparison with Porretta et al. (2020) succeeded and the secondary accent-model test is both missing the original finding in the text and declared inconclusive by the authors, the outcome is 'successful'.
